items.content_text:
Traders Beat the Models 133 to 31: Weather Is a Market Now

The forecast now has a price. Kalshi runs a market on each day's high temperature in 24 US cities, and a tracker that puts every market next to 82 weather model runs and the live thermometer reading that settles it found a clear winner in the first week: the traders were better forecasters in 133 of 164 markets.

Today's sharpest fight is Oklahoma City. Traders favor a high of 71 degrees or below at 61 cents, while the models lean toward 74 to 75 degrees at 33 percent and give the traders' pick only 13 percent, a 48-point gap between money and models. Austin is nearly as split: traders price 85 to 86 degrees at 60 cents, while the models favor 81 to 82 at 30 percent.

The pattern repeats across the board. In Washington, DC, traders price 65 to 66 degrees at 74 cents against a model reading of 40 percent for the same band. In New York City, traders favor 60 to 61 degrees at 55 cents while the models put that band at 37 percent. In Atlanta, both sides agree it stays cool, but traders are firmer: 63 degrees or below at 92 cents against the models at 84 percent.

That is the point of a weather market. A forecast model gives one answer for free; a market makes thousands of people pay to be wrong. When traders beat 82 model runs in 133 of 164 markets in a single week, the thermometer stops being just a weather story and becomes a scoreboard, settled every afternoon, city by city.

Sources: Weather Markets, Kalshi

items.content_text:
An Index for Everything: S&P Wants to Price the Future

The most important benchmark in finance is getting into the prediction business. On October 26, S&P Dow Jones Indices, the firm behind the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average, signed a multi-year partnership with Kalshi to build indices composed of Kalshi event contracts, and to let Kalshi list contracts on the S&P 500, the Dow and other S&P benchmarks that settle directly to official index data.

The scale of the incumbent is the point. By the end of 2024, more than $20 trillion was indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 alone. The Dow dates to 1896 and the S&P 500 to 1957. The new indices will bundle related event contracts, covering political power, supply chain risk, AI's impact on employment, sports outcomes and weather, into single indicators, the way a stock index bundles companies.

It is not the only door into finance opening. Rothera, the exchange owned 45 percent each by Robinhood and Susquehanna, has won CFTC approval for the first swap tied to a listed company's key performance indicator, starting with Tesla's earnings per share. The approval opens three families: financial reporting, covering earnings, sales, margins and expenses; platform usage, covering active users, customers, flights and trips; and production, covering units produced and delivered, rolling out gradually this autumn.

Kalshi is building from the other side, too: on October 6 it launched a perpetual future on 500 large U.S. companies, and last week it added sector KPI markets tracking corporate metrics across industries. Prediction markets began by pricing elections and games. Now they are pricing the earnings calendar, and Wall Street's own benchmark house is helping them do it.

items.content_text:
Ten Platforms, Zero Compliance: Ohio Goes to Court

On October 2, the Ohio Casino Control Commission sent cease-and-desist letters to ten prediction market platforms, ordering them to halt sports event contracts for users in the state: Coinbase, Gemini Titan, MooMoo Financial, Novig, Plus500US, Polymarket, ProphetX, Robinhood Derivatives, Underdog and WeBull Financial. Each had 14 days, until October 16, to confirm compliance in writing. None did, and Governor Mike DeWine has now said the state will file suit.

Ohio is not bluffing from a weak hand. On September 25, the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously in KalshiEx LLC v. Schuler that the Commodity Exchange Act neither applies to sports event contracts nor preempts Ohio's sports gaming law, rejecting the federal preemption argument the platforms rely on. Kalshi, fined $5 million by Ohio in April 2026 and already under a separate court order, asked the full Sixth Circuit to rehear the case on October 16. That petition is pending.

The threatened penalties are blunt: fines equal to the entire value of contracts offered to Ohioans, with unlicensed sports gaming treated as a felony that can constitute bookmaking, and officers, directors and parent companies in scope. Ohio has licensed sports betting since 2023; none of the ten holds a commission license. DeWine has called the products nothing more than gambling.

The map, though, is split. The same day Ohio sent its letters, a federal judge in Illinois ruled the opposite way, finding Kalshi's sports contracts are likely swaps under federal law. Kalshi and Polymarket have reportedly spent a combined $3 million fighting state restrictions. Ohio's suits will be the first real test of whether a state can enforce its gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges.

items.title: 87 Percent to Win, Three Spreads to Choose: Sunday's Margin Trade
items.content_text:
87 Percent to Win, Three Spreads to Choose: Sunday's Margin Trade

The winner is not really in dispute anywhere. For the 1 p.m. ET kickoff on Sunday, November 1, Kalshi has Cincinnati at 87%, Polymarket at 86%, DraftKings at -675 and the Dimers model at 87%, with a projected score of Bengals 30, Titans 17. A 1-6 Tennessee team visiting a 4-2 Cincinnati side chasing a third straight win is priced as close to settled.

What the markets cannot agree on is the margin. Kalshi traders have made 10.5 points the centre of the spread ladder, DraftKings sits at 12.5, and Polymarket's default line is 13.5. That is a three-point spread between the spreads, and for this game that gap is the whole trade.
